interactions.label: Why do submucosal fibroids most commonly cause menorrhagia?

params.question: Why do submucosal fibroids most commonly cause menorrhagia?

answers.text: They compress the uterine artery, reducing blood flow to the endometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Submucosal fibroids do not compress the uterine artery. Their effect is mechanical — on the endometrial cavity itself, not on the arterial supply.

answers.text: They distort the endometrial cavity and impair uterine contractility, enlarging the bleeding surface area

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Submucosal fibroids project into the endometrial cavity, increasing the surface area from which bleeding occurs and impairing the myometrium's ability to contract and arrest bleeding.

answers.text: They secrete oestrogen, directly stimulating excessive endometrial proliferation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fibroids are oestrogen-dependent (they grow under oestrogenic influence) but do not produce oestrogen themselves. The mechanism of menorrhagia is mechanical, not hormonal.

answers.text: They cause endometrial atrophy by compressing the basal layer of the endometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Submucosal fibroids actually increase the endometrial surface area rather than causing atrophy — this is precisely why bleeding is heavier.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pathophysiology: submucosal fibroids project into the endometrial cavity, enlarging the surface area from which bleeding occurs and mechanically impairing the uterine muscle's ability to contract and stop blood flow.
Well done. Understanding this mechanism explains why submucosal fibroids (FIGO types 0–2) cause the worst menorrhagia and why hysteroscopic resection is the surgical approach of choice for them.

params.question: What explains the development of stress urinary incontinence in a patient with uterine prolapse?

answers.text: Associated descent of the anterior vaginal wall (cystocele) displacing the bladder neck

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The anterior vaginal wall supports the bladder. When it descends (cystocele), the bladder neck loses its anatomical support, leading to involuntary leakage on coughing, sneezing, or straining.

answers.text: Detrusor muscle overactivity from direct compression of pelvic nerves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Detrusor overactivity can cause urge incontinence, but stress incontinence — leakage provoked by increased abdominal pressure — results from anatomical displacement of the bladder neck due to anterior wall descent.

answers.text: Chronic urinary tract infection secondary to exposed vaginal mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While recurrent UTIs can occur with advanced prolapse, stress incontinence is a mechanical problem caused by loss of anatomical support to the bladder neck, not by infection.

answers.text: Direct compression of the urethra by the descending uterus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In prolapse the uterus descends through the vagina. Urethral compression would actually impede flow (causing retention), not cause stress incontinence. The mechanism is loss of support via the cystocele.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: uterine prolapse rarely occurs in isolation. The anterior vaginal wall often descends with it (cystocele), displacing the bladder neck and causing stress urinary incontinence — leakage on coughing, sneezing, or straining.

Exactly. This is why the clinical assessment of prolapse includes evaluating each compartment separately — the anterior wall (cystocele), the uterus, and the posterior wall (rectocele) — since each produces its own symptom cluster.

interactions.label: Post-menopausal bleeding requires urgent investigation regardless of the amount

params.question: Post-menopausal bleeding requires urgent investigation regardless of the amount of bleeding.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. PMB is an absolute alarm symptom that mandates urgent investigation regardless of amount. A small spot of blood can be due to endometrial carcinoma — the volume of bleeding does not predict the severity of the underlying pathology.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. PMB is an absolute gynaecological alarm symptom. Even a tiny spot of blood noticed on toilet paper mandates investigation, because the amount of bleeding does not correlate with the severity of the underlying pathology — a small bleed can signal endometrial carcinoma.
